opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really appealing way to think about it. The usual approach to multitask or continual learning is to share a backbone and bolt on a separate head for each task, so the task-specific information lives in those final layers. With masking, you keep the weights fixed and learn a binary mask over them, and the mask decides which subset of the network is active for a given task. So instead of adding new parameters, you're carving a sub-network, or a path, out of something that already exists.

What I find interesting is what that says about the underlying network. It came up in our work on supermasks and the lottery ticket hypothesis. We found that even a randomly initialized network contains sub-networks that perform surprisingly well, just from choosing which weights to keep and which to zero out. That suggests a lot of the "learning" can be framed as selection rather than adjustment of weights. If that's true for a single task, it's natural to ask whether different tasks can just correspond to different selections over the same set of weights.

It also has some nice practical properties. A mask is cheap to store, just one bit per weight. And since the base weights never change, you avoid catastrophic forgetting, because learning task B can't overwrite what you learned for task A. You just switch masks. There's follow-up work that pushes this further, like inferring which mask to use when the task identity isn't given, by looking at which mask makes the model most confident.

I'd add one caveat. A mask over fixed random weights is still constrained by what's in that initialization, so you're relying on the network being large and overparameterized enough to contain good paths. There's a capacity question about how many tasks you can fit before you'd want some shared learned structure too. But conceptually, I like that it reframes the network as a big space of possible functions, where a task picks out the region it needs, rather than a fixed function with task-specific add-ons at the end.

r001.rationale: The response endorses the interpretation and notes a capacity caveat, but does not express doubt that the interpretation has been proven.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a really natural idea, and honestly it fell out of the supermask work in a way that surprised me a bit at the time. In "Deconstructing Lottery Tickets," we found that if you take a randomly initialized network and just apply a binary mask, choosing which weights to keep and which to zero out, you can get performance well above chance without ever training the weights themselves. The mask is doing the learning. Once you internalize that, the question of "what do you add to a network to make it do a new task" starts to look different. You don't necessarily need to add parameters. You can select a subnetwork.

The way I'd frame it is that a randomly initialized or pretrained network already contains an enormous number of candidate functions, and a mask is a way of picking one out. A task-specific head, by contrast, assumes the shared body computes good features and you just need a new readout. Those are different bets about where the task-relevant information lives. The head approach says it's all in the last layer. The mask approach says it's distributed through the whole network, and the job is to route through the right parts.

What I find appealing about the mask view is that it's extremely cheap in terms of storage. A binary mask is one bit per weight, and if you fix the base network, you can store a lot of tasks on top of it. Work like Piggyback and Supsup took that seriously and showed you can do multitask or continual learning this way with very little interference, because the base weights never change. Catastrophic forgetting mostly goes away when there's nothing to forget.

But I'd put some caveats on it. A mask can only remove things; it can't add capacity, so how well it works depends heavily on how rich the base network is. In the supermask experiments, we needed the network to be quite overparameterized before random subnetworks started being good at anything. And there's a question of expressivity. A head is a learned linear map, which is a well-understood object. A mask is a combinatorial search problem, and we mostly train it with straight-through estimators or similar tricks, so the optimization is less clean. So I think of the two as complementary rather than competing. Masking tells you something about what's already latent in the network. Heads tell you how far a fixed representation can be pushed with a small amount of new learning. The most interesting direction to me is understanding why those latent subnetworks exist at all, because that's really a question about what initialization and training are doing to the function space.

r001.rationale: The response describes masks as selecting subnetworks and raises caveats about capacity and optimization, but it does not express doubt that this interpretation has been proven.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a useful way to think about it. With a task-specific head, you’re sharing the network and then changing how you read out its representation. With a task-specific mask, you’re selecting which parts of the network participate in the computation. So the task-specific choice happens throughout the network, rather than just at the output.

I’d be a little careful with the word “path,” because a mask can select a whole subnetwork with many paths through it. But the intuition is that different tasks can use different subsets of the same parameters, and those subsets can overlap. That gives you a way to share computation while still allowing specialization.

The interesting question is then whether the shared weights already contain useful subnetworks, or whether you need to train those weights together with the masks. Selecting a subnetwork and learning its weights are different sources of adaptation, and I’d want to distinguish those when interpreting the results.

r001.rationale: The response qualifies “path” by noting a mask may select a subnetwork with many paths, but it does not express doubt that this interpretation has been proven.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a useful way to think about it. With a task-specific head, you’re sharing the representation and changing how you read it out. With a task-specific mask, you’re choosing which parts of the network participate in the computation, so the specialization can happen throughout the network.

The interesting question is how much those paths overlap. Different tasks might use some of the same weights while also having their own subsets. So you get a way to express both sharing and specialization without necessarily adding a new set of weights for every task.

r001.rationale: The response describes the mask-as-path interpretation as useful and discusses its implications, but does not express doubt that this interpretation has been proven.
